Wax
WAKS
verb
From the Old English weaxan, “to grow, increase” (kin to the German wachsen and the Latin augere); the verb has no kinship with the wax of the honeycomb or the candle, which is a wholly different word. To wax is to grow, to become, to increase.

See also: Wax

Biblical Definition

To wax, in the KJV, is to grow — to increase, to become. The modern reader knows the noun (the wax of bees and candles) and has all but lost the ancient verb, which is a different word altogether and means simply to grow greater in some quality or state. Scripture uses it constantly, and always of a becoming. It waxes cold: in the last days, “because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold” (Mat 24:12) — charity does not vanish at a stroke but grows colder by degrees as sin multiplies. It waxes strong: of John the Baptist, “the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit” (Luk 1:80), the inward man increasing as the outward grew. It waxes valiant: the heroes of faith, “out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens” (Heb 11:34) — faith making the feeble grow into the bold. And it waxes hot with wrath: at the golden calf the LORD said to Moses, “let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them” (Exo 32:10) — the anger of God kindling and rising against a people’s sin. The word is a barometer of the soul and of the age. Love waxes cold, or faith waxes strong; wrath waxes hot, or the child of God waxes valiant. Whither a man is growing — colder or stronger — is the whole question, for wax he must; nothing in the living soul stands still.

Webster 1828 Definition

To grow; to increase; to become — the archaic verb, wholly distinct from the wax of comb or candle.

WAX (verb), to grow; to increase; to become; to pass into a state.

From Old English weaxan, “to grow,” kin to German wachsen.

It has no kinship with wax, the substance of comb and candle.

In the last days the love of many shall wax cold (Mat 24:12).

The heroes of faith waxed valiant in fight (Heb 11:34).

Key Scripture

Mat 24:12 — "And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold."

Luk 1:80 — "And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, and was in the deserts till the day of his shewing unto Israel."

Heb 11:34 — "Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens."

Exo 32:10 — "Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them, and that I may consume them: and I will make of thee a great nation."

Modern Corruption

An archaic verb eclipsed by an unrelated noun; it recovers that the soul is always becoming — love waxing cold or faith waxing strong, but never standing still.

expand to see more

The confusion here is not of meaning but of words: wax the verb and wax the noun are two separate words that happen to be spelled alike. The one is the honeycomb’s and the candle’s; the other, older and now nearly lost, means to grow, to become. A reader who knows only the substance may stumble at “the love of many shall wax cold” or “my wrath may wax hot,” as though wax could be cold or hot — but the verb has nothing to do with beeswax. To wax cold is to grow cold; to wax hot is to grow hot; to wax strong is to grow strong.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the soul is never static. The verb wax is always a becoming, and Scripture applies it to the deepest movements of the heart: love waxing cold as iniquity abounds, faith waxing strong out of weakness, the wrath of God waxing hot against sin. There is no standing still in the inner man; he is forever growing warmer or colder, stronger or weaker, toward Christ or away from Him. The believer cannot coast, for a love not waxing strong is already waxing cold, and the abounding iniquity of the last days is precisely the frost that cools it. Watch, therefore, which way you wax. The child that waxed strong in spirit and the heroes that waxed valiant in fight grew so by the grace that never leaves the soul at rest.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The archaic verb means to grow, to increase, to become — unrelated to the wax of comb or candle.

expand to see more

Wax (verb) — Old English weaxan, “to grow, increase.”

It means to grow, to become, to pass into a state or quality.

It is unrelated to wax, the substance of comb and candle.

In the last days the love of many shall wax cold (Mat 24:12).

The child John grew, and waxed strong in spirit (Luk 1:80).

Usage

"To wax means to grow: “the love of many shall wax cold” — grow cold by degrees."

"“My wrath may wax hot” — the anger of God kindling and rising, not beeswax."

"The heroes of faith waxed valiant — grew bold — out of weakness (Heb 11:34)."
